questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Briefly discuss the evidences of Continental Drift.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Continental drift** is the idea put forward by **Alfred Wegener in 1912** that the continents were once joined in one super-continent, **Pangaea**, which broke up and whose parts moved apart to their present positions. The main evidences are the following.

1. **Fit of the continental margins (the jigsaw fit).** The coast of eastern South America fits that of West Africa, notably the bulge of Brazil into the Gulf of Guinea (and the Cameroon coast). The fit is better when the edges of the continental shelves (about the 500 fathom or 1 000 m depth contour), and not the shorelines, are matched (Bullard's computer fit, 1965), and North America, Greenland and Europe also fit.
2. **Matching rock types and structures across the oceans.** Old Precambrian shields and their ages, and mountain belts, continue from one continent to another when the continents are put together: for example the Appalachian and Caledonian belts of North America and Europe, and the Cape Fold Belt of South Africa with the Sierra de la Ventana of Argentina. The Pan-African (Brasiliano) belts of north-east Brazil continue into West and Central Africa.
3. **Fossil evidence.** The same **land plants and animals** are found in rocks of the same age on continents now separated by oceans, which they could not have crossed: the seed fern **Glossopteris** in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, the freshwater reptile **Mesosaurus** (Permian) in Brazil and South Africa only, and the land reptiles **Lystrosaurus** and **Cynognathus** in Africa, India and Antarctica.
4. **Palaeoclimatic evidence.** Permo-Carboniferous **glacial deposits (tillites)** and striated pavements are found in South America, southern Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, now in warm latitudes, and their ice-flow directions radiate from a centre in Gondwana when the continents are joined. Coal beds of tropical origin occur in Antarctica and in high-latitude areas such as Spitsbergen, and desert sandstones and evaporites occur at present high latitudes, so that the continents must have changed latitude.
5. **Palaeomagnetism.** The magnetisation fixed in rocks gives the position of the magnetic pole at the time. The **polar wandering paths** obtained from different continents do not agree, but they coincide when the continents are moved back together, which shows that the continents have moved relative to each other.
6. **Sea floor spreading and ocean floor data (supporting evidence).** Symmetrical **magnetic stripes** (normal and reversed polarity) on both sides of the mid-oceanic ridges, the ocean floor getting **older away from the ridges** (nowhere older than about 180 million years), thin sediments near the ridges, and the present movement of the plates measured by **GPS and satellite laser ranging**, give the mechanism which Wegener lacked.

(A neat sketch of the continents of Gondwana and Laurasia fitted together, showing the distribution of Glossopteris and the ice-sheet, is credited.)
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) List THREE factors that influence the violence of a volcanic eruption.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Three factors that influence the violence (explosiveness) of a volcanic eruption are:

1. **The viscosity of the magma**, which depends on its **silica content** and its temperature. A silica-rich (acid, rhyolitic) magma is cool and very viscous, so that gas cannot escape easily and the eruption is violent; a basic (basaltic) magma is hot and fluid, and the eruption is gentle.
2. **The gas (volatile) content of the magma**, mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur gases. A high dissolved gas content expands violently as the magma rises and the pressure falls, and shatters the magma into ash and pumice.
3. **The ease and the speed of escape of the gas**, which depends on the blocking of the vent by a plug of solidified lava, on the **rate of ascent of the magma**, and on the contact of the magma with groundwater or sea water (steam explosions). A blocked vent lets the pressure rise until it bursts explosively.

**Acid igneous rocks** are igneous rocks with a **high silica content, more than 66 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$** (acid rocks, in the older classification, 66 to 75 per cent), and with free quartz. They are called **felsic** (feldspar and silica) and are light in colour (**leucocratic**). The main types are **granite** and **granodiorite** (plutonic), **microgranite** and **granite porphyry** (hypabyssal), **pegmatite** and **aplite** (vein rocks) and **rhyolite**, **obsidian** and **pumice** (volcanic).

**(i) Composition.**
- **Chemical:** more than 66 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, rich in $\mathrm{Na_2O}$, $\mathrm{K_2O}$ and $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, and poor in Fe, Mg and Ca.
- **Mineral:** **quartz** (about 20 to 40 per cent, and always more than 10 per cent), **alkali feldspars** (orthoclase, microcline) generally more abundant than **sodium-rich plagioclase** (albite-oligoclase); **micas** (muscovite and biotite) and sometimes a little **hornblende** as the dark (mafic) minerals, which are less than 15 to 20 per cent; accessory minerals are zircon, apatite, magnetite and tourmaline.
- **Physical:** low density (about 2.6 to 2.7 g per cubic centimetre), light grey, pink or white in colour. They crystallise at the lower end of Bowen's reaction series, from magmas at about 650 to 800 degrees Celsius.

**(ii) Texture.**
- **Granite (plutonic): phaneritic, holocrystalline, medium- to coarse-grained, equigranular** (granitic texture) with interlocking crystals which grew slowly at depth; **porphyritic granite** has large feldspar phenocrysts in a coarse groundmass; **pegmatite** is very coarse (crystals of centimetres to metres, sometimes with graphic intergrowths of quartz and feldspar).
- **Microgranite and granite porphyry (hypabyssal):** fine- to medium-grained, or porphyritic.
- **Rhyolite (volcanic): aphanitic (fine-grained, cryptocrystalline), often porphyritic** with phenocrysts of quartz and feldspar in a fine groundmass, and flow banding; **obsidian** is **glassy** (conchoidal fracture, no crystals); **pumice** is **vesicular**, a frothy glass full of gas holes; **spherulitic** texture also occurs.

**(iii) Mode of occurrence.**
- **Intrusive (plutonic):** as **batholiths** (very large masses of granite, the cores of fold mountain belts), **stocks and bosses**; in the **hypabyssal** zone as **dykes, sills** and ring dykes of microgranite and porphyry; **pegmatite and aplite veins** in the roof and the country rocks of granite. Granites are the commonest rocks of the continental crust and are found in the crystalline (Precambrian) basement of Africa, including Cameroon, and in the cores of the old mountain chains.
- **Extrusive (volcanic):** as **rhyolite lava flows** and **domes** (the lava is so viscous that it forms thick domes and short flows, with obsidian at the surface), as **ash-flow tuffs and welded ignimbrites**, and as **pumice and ash falls** in explosive (Plinian) eruptions; they are associated with destructive plate margins and continental crust.
- They contact their country rocks with **chilled margins** and a **contact metamorphic aureole**, and are cut by veins of quartz and minerals of economic value (tin, tungsten, gold, kaolin from weathered granite).
